client: I've been really struggling lately with everything piling up at work. They just handed me this massive project with an insane deadline, and of course it had to happen right when half my team is out, so I'm basically doing everything myself. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the work is still going to be there when I leave this office.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying an enormous amount right now — the pressure of that project, doing the work of multiple people, and on top of that, a part of you is wondering if even being here can make a dent in it. That kind of exhaustion can make it hard to feel hopeful about anything offering relief. I'm curious — when you say talking might not change anything, is that a thought that tends to show up for you in other areas too, or does it feel more specific to how overwhelmed you are right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I think it shows up in other areas too, but right now it feels extra loud because I'm so buried in this work stuff. Like, I've tried venting to friends before and they just say "that sounds rough" and move on, so I've kind of learned that talking doesn't really lead anywhere. I guess I'm just not sure what you're supposed to do with all this that actually makes a difference.
therapist: It makes a lot of sense that you'd feel skeptical when past experiences have taught you that sharing doesn't lead to much — that's not a pessimistic quirk, it's actually a reasonable conclusion you drew from real evidence. What's interesting to me is that even with that doubt, you're still here, which tells me some part of you is still reaching for something different. I wonder — when you imagine what "actually making a difference" would look like, what comes to mind?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess "making a difference" would look like... not feeling this constant knot in my stomach every time I think about work, or at least feeling like I can actually get through the day without dreading every email notification. But honestly, even saying that out loud feels kind of pointless, because the project deadlines aren't going to change and my team members aren't magically coming back. I don't know, maybe I'm just looking for someone to tell me it's going to be okay, even though I know that's not really how it works.
therapist: You just painted a really clear picture of what relief could feel like — that knot loosening, moving through your day without bracing for the next thing — and that's actually worth holding onto, because it tells us something important about what matters to you. I notice that even as you described it, there was something in your voice that sounded almost rushed, like you were quickly closing the door on the hope before it could fully land. What do you think happens for you when you let yourself want something like that — even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think when I let myself want something like that, I end up feeling worse if it doesn't happen, so it's almost safer to just not go there. It's like I've gotten so used to bracing for things to fall apart at work that hoping feels like setting myself up to be disappointed. And honestly, right now with this project, it feels almost irresponsible to even think about relief when there's still so much I have to get done.
therapist: What you're describing — keeping hope at arm's length to protect yourself from disappointment — is such a human response, and it makes complete sense given what you've been through. But I'm struck by something: you've framed hoping as almost selfish or irresponsible right now, like you don't deserve relief until the work is done, and I'm curious whether that belief might actually be adding to the weight you're carrying rather than helping you get through it. What do you think — is there a part of you that feels like you have to earn the right to feel okay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually hit a little harder than I expected, because yeah, I think that's exactly what's going on. Like, there's this voice in my head that says I don't get to relax or feel better until everything is finished and done perfectly, and if I take a breath before then, I'm being lazy or letting people down. But even recognizing that right now, I don't really know how to turn that voice off, especially when the deadlines are real and the pressure isn't just in my head.
therapist: That voice you're describing — the one that ties your worth to completion and perfection — is one of the most exhausting things a person can carry, and just naming it so clearly is actually a meaningful step. The goal isn't necessarily to silence it overnight, but to start noticing when it's running the show and gently questioning whether it's telling you the truth — because "taking a breath" and "letting people down" aren't actually the same thing, even if that voice insists they are. What do you think that voice learned, or where do you think it came from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean, probably from growing up in a house where things were kind of unpredictable, and doing well at school or finishing my chores perfectly was one of the ways I could feel like I had some control. My parents weren't bad people, but praise was pretty rare and criticism came a lot faster, so I think I just learned that good enough was never really enough. It's weird to connect that to a work deadline in 2024, but sitting here I can kind of see how it's the same feeling.
therapist: What you just connected is really profound — that little kid who learned to find safety in perfection is still working so hard to protect you, just in a different setting now. I notice you said it feels "weird" to make that link, but there's actually something that sounds almost like relief in the way you're talking about it, like a piece of a puzzle clicking into place. Does it feel at all different, carrying this deadline, now that you can see where that pressure is really coming from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It does feel a little different, like maybe the deadline itself isn't the whole problem, which is kind of a relief but also almost more complicated in a way. Because if it's coming from this deeper place, that means it's not just going to go away when this project is done, and there will just be the next thing and the next thing after that. I guess I'm sitting with this weird mix of feeling understood for the first time in a while, but also a little scared about what that actually means for me going forward.
therapist: That mix you're describing — relief and fear sitting right next to each other — actually makes a lot of sense, because you've just realized the finish line you've been running toward was never going to give you what you were really looking for. And I notice there's something almost energized in the way you're talking about it, like this realization is landing with some real weight rather than just floating by. That fear you're feeling about "what this means going forward" — I'd gently say that's not a bad sign, it might actually be the first time you're facing the real thing instead of just the deadline.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I think you're right that this feels different from just stressing about a deadline, but I also don't really know what to do with that realization when I walk out of here and my inbox is still full. Like, understanding where it comes from doesn't automatically make it easier to not check my email at midnight or stop feeling guilty when I'm not working. I want to believe this is actually going somewhere useful, but I'm not sure how you get from this kind of insight to actually changing how you feel day to day.
therapist: You're asking exactly the right question, and it's worth saying that insight is genuinely just the starting point — the real work is building small, concrete moments where you practice *not* listening to that voice, even when it's loud. What you're describing, the midnight emails, the guilt when you rest, those are actually very specific habits we can work with, not just feelings to push through. I'm curious — if you imagine one small moment tomorrow where you could test what it feels like to put the phone down *before* the voice says it's okay, what would that moment look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I can picture maybe after dinner, like around 9pm, putting my phone in another room instead of keeping it next to me on the couch. But honestly, just imagining that makes me anxious, because what if something urgent comes in and I miss it, and then tomorrow is even worse because I wasn't on top of it. I think that's exactly the voice you're talking about, but knowing that doesn't make the anxiety any less real in the moment.
therapist: You just did something really important — you named the exact moment the voice shows up and what it says, which means you're already one step ahead of it. That anxiety is real, and we're not trying to pretend it away, but it's worth noticing that the "what if something urgent comes in" thought is the voice's best argument, not necessarily the truth — how many times has a genuine emergency actually arrived in your inbox after 9pm? That one small experiment, phone in the other room after dinner, could be less about solving the anxiety and more about gathering your own evidence that you can survive the discomfort.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: When you put it that way, like gathering evidence rather than fixing everything at once, it feels slightly less overwhelming, but I'm still not totally convinced one night of putting my phone down is going to quiet years of this pattern. And if I'm being honest, I'm already thinking about how I'll probably just sit there on the couch anxious the whole time, which doesn't exactly sound like rest. I guess I'm wondering if the discomfort is actually worth it, or if I'll just end up more wound up than if I'd checked my phone.
therapist: You're absolutely right that one night won't undo years of this pattern, and I don't want to oversell it — but I'm also noticing something in how you're describing the experiment, there's almost an anticipation in your voice, like part of you is already leaning toward trying it even as another part is talking you out of it. The discomfort you're predicting — sitting anxious on the couch — is actually the exact same feeling you're already living with when you *do* check your phone, so in a way you're not risking more discomfort, just a different relationship to it. What if the goal for that hour isn't to feel restful, but just to prove to yourself that you can tolerate the anxiety without needing to act on it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
